doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Rock and roll backbeats and Charlie Watts
summary: Monk asks about Butch's early dislike of rock and roll beats; Butch spells out the patterns and praises classic simple grooves.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Okay. Well I was going to ask you about that, but first I wanted to — there’s been this odd thing on my mind sort of since that interview. You said early on when you were learning the drums and the music that was being played on the radio was, you know, late 50s, early 60s rock & roll. And you didn’t care for it that much because it boom-whack- whack-boom-boom. So just to clear it up for me, was that boom-whack-whack-boom- boom? Or boom-whack-whack-boom-BOOM?
Actually you’re leaving out a whack. It was whack-whack-boom-boom-whack.
Or, if you really felt adventurous, it was boom-whack-boom-boom-whack-whack. Or boom-whack-whack-boom-whack-boom-whack, which, to his credit, Charlie Watts still plays, to this day.

No, no. I mean there are sometimes when just the oldies and the goodies are the only thing that will really fit the bill you know. So you can’t go wrong sometimes with just going boom-whack-boom-boom-whack. That’s it.
Be sure to tell your students that, will ya?
I usually do but they forget it. They’re off on more adventurous trips than I am.
